extracted.intended_audience: writers and critics of satire, comic essayists, and readers interested in humorous/social satire
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing ridicule in writing (comedy, burlesque) and for using comic devices (character via eyes, vocal 'cries' etc.) in satirical essays and sketches. Covers choice of form, characterization by gesture/glance, and performative aspects of street-voices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Branches of Ridicule: Comedy vs Burlesque
rubrics_metrics.description: The two great Branches of Ridicule in Writing are Comedy and Burlesque. The first ridicules Persons by drawing them in their proper Characters, the other by drawing them quite unlike themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comedy when you aim to expose follies by portraying people in their true character; use burlesque when you wish to ridicule by incongruity—representing persons out of character. Examples given: Don Quixote (mean person in heroic accoutrements) and Lucian's Gods (great persons represented as basest among the people).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtypes of Burlesque (two modes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Burlesque is therefore of two kinds; the first represents mean Persons in the Accoutrements of Heroes, the other describes great Persons acting and speaking like the basest among the People.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether your burlesque will 'raise' the low by clothing them in heroic form (comic contrast from elevation) or 'pull down' the high by exposing base behaviour in lofty figures (satirical debasement). Use concrete examples to make the incongruity recognisable to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form/Measure choice: Heroick verse vs Doggerel
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the low Character is to be raised, the Heroick is the proper Measure; but when an Hero is to be pulled down and degraded, it is done best in Doggerel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match verse/form to the satirical intent: heroic pomp (grand measure) heightens the absurdity of lifting the low; doggerel or rough verse is apt for debasing or caricaturing the great. Consider audience taste too (e.g. readers fond of double rhymes may prefer doggerel). Example: Hudibras (doggerel) vs what it might have been in heroic verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance raillery (wit) with good sense
rubrics_metrics.description: We meet with more Raillery among the Moderns, but more Good Sense among the Ancients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware mere sharpness of raillery (surface wit) that lacks underlying sense or moral weight. Effective ridicule combines wit with discernment and 'good sense'—not merely abusive or empty mockery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of metaphor and recurring imagery (laughter as amiable)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Metaphor of Laughing, applied to Fields and Meadows when they are in Flower, or to Trees when they are in Blossom, runs through all Languages... This shews that we naturally regard Laughter, as what is in it self both amiable and beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ widely-recognised metaphors (e.g., laughter as beauty/flowering) to evoke agreeable, universal responses. Familiar metaphors can lend warmth and acceptance to comic passages rather than mere derision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization by the eye (eyes as seat of passions)
rubrics_metrics.description: That fine Part of our Constitution seems as much the Receptacle and Seat of our Passions, Appetites and Inclinations as the Mind it self; and at least it is the outward Portal to introduce them to the House within...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ocular description (glances, looks, eye-movements) to convey emotions, desires, pride, anger, avarice, and other passions succinctly—often more effectively than dialogue. Small ocular details may communicate large interior states in comedy and satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typology of eyes and glance-types as character shorthand
rubrics_metrics.description: Names, Colours, Qualities, and Turns of Eyes vary... notable are those that borrow their Titles from Animals... a greedy rapacious Aspect takes its Name from the Cat, that of a sharp piercing Nature from the Hawk, those of an amorous roguish Look derive their Title even from the Sheep...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy established ocular metaphors (e.g., 'hawk's eye', 'sheep's eye', 'cat-like glance') to quickly signal character traits or comic dispositions. Classical/mythical exemplars (Argus, Janus, the Sun-Proof Eye) can be used for heightened or humorous effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glances and ocular gestures as social/situational signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Oblique Vision, when natural, was anciently the Mark of Bewitchery and magical Fascination... when 'tis forced and affected it carries a wanton Design, and in Play-houses, and other publick Places, this ocular Intimation is often an Assignation for bad Practices: ... Tipping the Wink, the Circumspective Rowl, the Side-peep through a thin Hood or Fan, must be put in the Class of Heteropticks...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use variations in glances—oblique looks, winks, side-peeps—as conventional signals in scenes of intrigue, flirtation, or deceit. Be mindful of whether the glance is natural or affected; its comic or sinister meaning depends on that distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal and moral judgment of staring (social impropriety)
rubrics_metrics.description: Starers, who disturb whole Assemblies without any Regard to Time, Place or Modesty... a Starer is not usually a Person to be convinced by Reason of the Thing, nor so easily rebuked, as to amend by Admonitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In social satire, mark staring as an impolite, intrusive trait to be mocked or corrected. Devices (literal or dramatic) to prevent staring (e.g., perspective-glasses) can be introduced for satirical effect or as comedic inventions that reveal social norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulate instrumental cries: tune and licensing
rubrics_metrics.description: No Instrument of this Nature should be made use of, which I have not tuned and licensed, after having carefully examined in what manner it may affect the Ears of her Majesty's liege Subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting street music or background sound in comic writing, control the instruments' timbre and tuning to achieve the intended comedic or picturesque effect. Untuned or chaotic instrumentation can be used deliberately for comic disorder, but consider audience weariness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt vocal 'cries' to the wares: pitch, timbre and phrase should fit the product
rubrics_metrics.description: I would... sweeten and mellow the Voices of these itinerant Tradesmen, before they make their Appearance in our Streets; as also to accommodate their Cries to their respective Wares; and to take care in particular, that those may not make the most Noise who have the least to sell...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the vendor's vocal line fit the commodity for comic verisimilitude (e.g., grave, slow tones for heavy goods; bright, sharp notes for light items). Use mismatch intentionally for humour (e.g., tiny wares sold with bombastic cries) but be aware of the satirical message (greed, vanity, absurdity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe time and measure in vocal delivery (tempo/urgency)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no just Time nor Measure observed in them. Our News should indeed be published in a very quick Time... It should not, however, be cried with the same Precipitation as Fire... I would... regulate in such a manner, that there should be some Distinction made between the spreading of a Victory, a March, or an Incampment...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control tempo and urgency in spoken or shouted comic lines: perishable or urgent news merits brisk tempo; false alarms or trivial matters should not mimic high alarm. Distinguish levels of urgency to create comedic irony or social commentary (overreaction vs understatement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity vs tune: avoid incomprehensible cries
rubrics_metrics.description: That idle Accomplishment which they all of them aim at, of Crying so as not to be understood... People know the Wares they deal in rather by their Tunes than by their Words... a Country Boy run out to buy Apples of a Bellows-mender, and Gingerbread from a Grinder of Knives and Scissars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that, even when using musical or stylised vocalizations for comic effect, readers/listeners can infer meaning; unintelligible performance can be funny when deliberate (comic misunderstanding), but overuse makes scenes useless or confusing. Use misrecognition as a comic device sparingly and with clear payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reuse and adapt popular tunes pragmatically
rubrics_metrics.description: I am always pleased with that particular Time of the Year which is proper for the pickling of Dill and Cucumbers; but alas, this Cry... is not heard above two Months. It would therefore be worth while to consider, whether the same Air might not in some Cases be adapted to other Words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recycling a familiar melodic phrase for different goods or occasions can create comic familiarity or satire (e.g., seasonal tunes used out of season), and can be a device to comment on repetitiveness or commercial opportunism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attitude toward vendors' inventive tunes and novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: It might likewise deserve our most serious Consideration, how far... those Humourists are to be tolerated, who... have invented particular Songs and Tunes of their own: Such as... the Pastryman, commonly known by the Name of the Colly-Molly-Puff; and such as is at this Day the Vender of Powder and Wash-balls, who... goes under the Name of Powder-Watt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting novel or eccentric vocal inventions, weigh their comic value against social disorder: inventive jingles can be endearing or ridiculous. Decide in narration whether to celebrate this individuality (comic colour) or to satirize it as tasteless affectation.
